body:
What does a distance–time graph show?

A distance–time graph represents how the cumulative distance travelled by an object changes with time. Time is plotted on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.

The shape and slope of the graph provide information about the object's speed. Such a graph makes it possible to compare motion during different time intervals.

Slope represents speed

The slope of a distance–time graph is the change in distance divided by the corresponding change in time.

$$\text{Average speed over an interval}=\frac{d_2-d_1}{t_2-t_1}$$

If distance increases by 20 m during 4 s, the average speed is \(20/4=5\) m/s. A steeper rising line indicates a higher speed than a less steep rising line, provided both graphs use the same axis scales.

Interpretation of common graph shapes

  • Straight rising line: Distance increases uniformly with time, showing constant speed over that interval.
  • Horizontal line: Distance remains unchanged while time passes, so the object is at rest during that interval.
  • Changing slope or a curved line: Speed is changing, indicating non-uniform motion.

Worked example: Motion with a halt

Consider an object whose cumulative distance readings are as follows.

Time (s)Distance (m)
00
210
420
620
830

Assume the object moves at constant speed between consecutive readings. From 0 s to 4 s, it covers 20 m in 4 s, giving 5 m/s. From 4 s to 6 s, the distance remains 20 m, indicating a halt for 2 s. From 6 s to 8 s, it covers another 10 m in 2 s, again giving 5 m/s.

For the complete 8 s journey, the total distance is 30 m and the average speed is \(30/8=3.75\) m/s. Thus, the average speed for the whole journey differs from the speed during the moving intervals.

A common graph confusion

A graph of cumulative distance travelled cannot slope downward because previously travelled distance is not lost when the object turns back. A position–time graph, however, can slope downward when position decreases along the selected positive axis.

For example, a person walking back towards the origin may have decreasing position while cumulative distance continues increasing.

The slope of a distance–time graph gives speed. The area under a distance–time graph is not used to calculate displacement in the standard school-level equations of motion.

Prelims focus

  • Time is on the horizontal axis; distance is on the vertical axis.
  • Slope of a distance–time graph represents speed.
  • A straight rising line indicates uniform speed.
  • A horizontal line indicates rest.
  • A changing slope indicates non-uniform speed.
  • Trap: A returning object can have decreasing position but not decreasing cumulative distance.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 13, 'Motion and Time', section 13.5, pp. 151–155, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', section 8.4.1, pp. 104–105, 2018–19 print.]

pictures.alt: Distance rises at 5 m/s from 0–4 s, stays at 20 m from 4–6 s, then rises at 5 m/s to 30 m at 8 s; average speed is 3.75 m/s.
pictures.caption: The horizontal portion shows the interval during which the object is at rest.

title: Distance–Time Graphs: Identifying Speed and Rest

body:
Understanding a velocity–time graph

A velocity–time graph shows how the velocity of an object changes with time. Time is represented on the horizontal axis and velocity on the vertical axis.

Unlike a distance–time graph, a velocity–time graph provides direct information about acceleration. It can also be used to calculate displacement.

Slope gives acceleration

The slope is calculated by dividing the change in velocity by the corresponding time interval.

$$a=\frac{v_2-v_1}{t_2-t_1}$$

  • Horizontal line: Constant velocity and zero acceleration.
  • Straight line with positive slope: Constant positive acceleration.
  • Straight line with negative slope: Constant negative acceleration.
  • Curved line: Acceleration is changing with time.

A line below the time axis represents motion in the negative direction. Its slope still determines acceleration.

Area gives displacement

The signed area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis gives displacement over the selected interval.

When velocity is positive, the area above the time axis contributes positive displacement. When velocity is negative, the area below the time axis contributes negative displacement.

If velocity remains positive throughout an interval, the displacement is equal to the distance travelled during that interval.

Worked example: Acceleration followed by uniform motion

An object begins with velocity 2 m/s at 0 s, increases uniformly to 6 m/s at 4 s and then continues at 6 m/s until 6 s.

During the first 4 s, acceleration is:

$$a=\frac{6-2}{4}=1\ \text{m/s}^2$$

The displacement during this interval equals the area of the trapezium under the graph:

$$s_1=\frac{2+6}{2}\times4=16\ \text{m}$$

During the next 2 s, velocity is constant at 6 m/s:

$$s_2=6\times2=12\ \text{m}$$

Total displacement is \(16+12=28\) m. Because velocity remains positive, the total distance travelled is also 28 m.

What happens when velocity becomes negative?

Suppose an object moves along a straight line with velocity +2 m/s at 0 s. Its velocity decreases uniformly to 0 m/s at 2 s and continues to −2 m/s at 4 s. Its acceleration remains −1 m/s2.

From 0 s to 2 s, the triangular area above the time axis represents +2 m displacement. From 2 s to 4 s, the triangular area below the axis represents −2 m displacement.

The total displacement is \(+2-2=0\) m, but the total distance travelled is \(2+2=4\) m. The object returns to its starting position.

For a velocity–time graph, add areas with their signs to find displacement. Add the magnitudes of the areas to find distance travelled.

Prelims focus

  • The slope of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.
  • A horizontal velocity–time graph indicates zero acceleration.
  • The signed area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.
  • A line below the time axis represents negative velocity.
  • Trap: A negative velocity does not mean negative speed.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', sections 8.4.2 and 8.5, pp. 105–109, 2018–19 print; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 'Motion', sections on graphical representation and equations of motion, consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Velocity rises from 2 to 6 m/s over 0–4 s, then stays constant to 6 s. Slopes give accelerations 1 and 0 m/s²; shaded areas give 16 m and 12 m, totaling 28 m.
pictures.caption: The slope gives acceleration, while the area under the graph gives displacement.

pictures.alt: Velocity falls from +2 to −2 m/s, reversing at 2 s. Areas +2 m and −2 m cancel, giving 0 m displacement but 4 m distance.
pictures.caption: Positive and negative areas cancel for displacement, although distance continues to accumulate.

title: Velocity–Time Graphs: Acceleration, Displacement and Direction

body:
What is uniform circular motion?

Uniform circular motion occurs when an object moves along a circular path at a constant speed. A runner following a circular track at steady speed is one example.

The object covers equal distances along the circular path in equal intervals of time. However, its direction of motion changes continuously.

Why is velocity not constant?

Velocity has both magnitude and direction. In uniform circular motion, the magnitude of velocity, which is speed, remains constant. Its direction changes at every point along the circular path.

Because velocity changes, the object has acceleration even though its speed does not change.

Uniform circular motion is accelerated motion. Constant speed does not imply zero acceleration when direction is changing.

Direction of velocity and force

At any point on a circular path, the instantaneous velocity is directed along the tangent to the circle at that point.

To maintain circular motion, a net force must act towards the centre of the circular path. This inward force changes the direction of velocity. The inward force is called the centripetal force; it is the net inward force supplied by an actual interaction, such as tension or friction.

If the inward force suddenly stops acting, the object initially continues along the tangent at its point of release. Other forces, if present, may subsequently change that path.

Speed in a circular path

For a circle of radius \(r\), the length of 1 complete round is its circumference, \(2\pi r\). If the object completes 1 round in time \(T\), called its time period, its speed is:

$$v=\frac{2\pi r}{T}$$

Here, \(r\) is measured in metres and \(T\) in seconds, so speed is measured in m/s.

Suppose a runner moves at constant speed around a circular track of radius 7 m and completes 1 round in 44 s. The speed is \(v=\frac{2\pi\times7}{44}\), which is approximately 1 m/s.

Distance and displacement after a complete round

After 1 complete circular round, the distance travelled is \(2\pi r\), but the displacement is zero because the object returns to its starting position. Consequently, average velocity over the complete round is zero, while average speed remains positive.

This connects circular motion with the distinction between speed and velocity: the object can maintain constant speed while its instantaneous velocity changes and its average velocity over a complete round is zero.

Prelims focus

  • Uniform circular motion means constant speed along a circular path.
  • Velocity changes because its direction changes.
  • Acceleration and the required net force point towards the centre.
  • Instantaneous velocity is tangent to the circular path.
  • Speed for 1 round is \(2\pi r/T\).
  • Trap: After 1 complete round, displacement is zero but distance is the circumference.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 8, 'Motion', section 8.6, pp. 110–112, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 10, 'Motion and Measurement of Distances', section 10.8, pp. 103–105, 2018–19 print.]

pictures.alt: An athlete in a teal shirt runs around a curved terracotta track at a public sports ground in present-day India.
pictures.caption: A runner following a circular track must continuously change direction.

pictures.alt: At P and Q, velocity is tangent to a counterclockwise circular path and net force points inward; release at P gives initial upward motion.
pictures.caption: Instantaneous velocity is tangential, while the required net force points towards the centre.

title: Uniform Circular Motion: Constant Speed with Changing Velocity

body:
Force is an interaction

A force is a push or pull produced through an interaction between objects. A force may start or stop motion, increase or decrease speed, change the direction of motion or change an object's shape.

Force has both magnitude and direction. Its SI unit is the newton (N).

Forces can be grouped into contact and non-contact forces. A person pushing a box and friction between surfaces are examples of contact forces. Gravity and magnetic attraction are examples of non-contact forces.

Balanced and unbalanced forces

Several forces may act on the same object simultaneously. Their combined effect is called the net force or resultant force.

Consider 2 horizontal forces acting on a box. If 5 N acts to the right and 5 N to the left, the forces balance and the net horizontal force is zero. If 8 N acts to the right and 3 N to the left, the net horizontal force is 5 N to the right.

Balanced forces do not change the velocity of an object. They may nevertheless change its shape, as when a soft object is squeezed from opposite sides.

Unbalanced forces cause acceleration. Depending on their direction, they may increase or decrease speed or change the direction of motion.

Zero net force does not necessarily mean zero velocity. An object may remain at rest or continue moving in a straight line at constant velocity.

Newton's first law of motion

Newton's first law of motion states that an object remains at rest or continues to move with uniform velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force.

This law explains why a force is needed to change motion rather than to maintain uniform straight-line motion.

For example, a ball rolling on the ground eventually stops because friction and other resistive forces oppose its motion. If those opposing forces were absent and the net external force were zero, the ball would continue with unchanged velocity.

Inertia and mass

Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion. The first law is therefore also known as the law of inertia.

Mass is a measure of inertia. A more massive object generally requires a greater net force to produce the same acceleration as a less massive object.

A loaded trolley has more inertia than an empty trolley of the same kind. Similarly, changing the speed of a heavy truck is more difficult than changing the speed of a small toy cart under comparable conditions.

Everyday examples of inertia

  • Bus starting suddenly: The feet of a standing passenger move forward with the bus, while the upper body initially tends to remain at rest. The passenger may lean backwards relative to the bus.
  • Bus stopping suddenly: The feet slow with the bus, while the upper body tends to continue moving forward. The passenger may lean forwards.
  • Car turning sharply: The body tends to continue along its previous straight-line path. The seat or side support must exert a force to change its direction.
  • Seat belt: A seat belt exerts the force needed to slow the passenger during sudden braking, reducing uncontrolled forward movement.

Galileo Galilei's study of motion helped establish the idea that an object does not require a continuous net force merely to keep moving uniformly. Isaac Newton expressed this principle in his first law.

Prelims focus

  • Force is a push or pull arising from interaction.
  • Balanced forces have zero net force.
  • Unbalanced net force produces acceleration.
  • Newton's first law is the law of inertia.
  • Mass measures inertia; its SI unit is kilogram (kg).
  • Trap: A moving object does not require a non-zero net force to maintain constant velocity.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 11, 'Force and Pressure', sections 11.1–11.5, pp. 127–134, 2018–19 print; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 9, 'Force and Laws of Motion', sections 9.1–9.3, pp. 114–118, 2018–19 print.]

pictures.caption: Equal opposite forces balance; unequal opposite forces produce a net force.

title: Force, Balanced Forces, Inertia and Newton's First Law
